concepts.name: Algorithmic management
concepts.description: Software algorithms assume managerial functions such as assigning, evaluating, and pricing work tasks.

concepts.name: Workplace consent
concepts.description: Individuals' enthusiastic and active participation to align their efforts with managerial objectives.

concepts.name: Engagement tactics
concepts.description: Workers interact within the boundaries of the algorithmic management system and generally follow the algorithm's nudges.

concepts.name: Deviance tactics
concepts.description: Workers manipulate their input into the algorithmic management system, pushing against its boundaries.

concepts.name: Good bad job
concepts.description: Work that is structurally problematic or precarious but is attractive and meaningful to workers.

claims: The shift from human managers to algorithmic managers on digital platforms manufactures workplace consent.
Workers navigate algorithmic management using engagement and deviance tactics.
Both engagement and deviance tactics elicit consent and contribute to workers seeing themselves as skillful agents.
Algorithmic management elicits consent through a series of narrow yet frequent choices that are associated with workers' sense of mastery.
Choice-based consent can mask the more structurally problematic elements of precarious on-demand work.
summary: This article explores how algorithmic management on digital platforms manufactures workplace consent, focusing on the ride-hailing industry. Drawing on a seven-year qualitative study, the author finds that workers make frequent, narrow choices within a highly confined system using engagement and deviance tactics. Both sets of tactics elicit active participation from workers, align their efforts with managerial objectives, and foster a sense of mastery, masking the precarious nature of the work and contributing to the appeal of what the author calls the 'good bad' job.
